newsitem.title: UK: Commodity funds prepare for 1997 market growth.
newsitem.headline: Commodity funds prepare for 1997 market growth.

text.p: Industrial commodities and funds that invest in them should both benefit from an uptick in world economic activity next year, said London-based fund managers. A four-percent growth rate is forecast for OECD countries in 1997 and expansion may be faster in China, Russia and some of the smaller Asian boom economies.
But the sources said buoyant raw material demand does not mean that investment funds will be piling a lot of money into positions in markets such items as gold, copper and crude oil.

UK-based "natural resource" fund managers, for instance, tend to buy equities in mining or oil producing companies -- although recently they have also had the opportunity to position their funds against indices weighted to a basket of commodities.
Increasingly in the past couple of years, the Goldman Sachs Commodity Index has provided a basis on which resource funds like Barclays Global Investors operate.
The Goldman Sachs index includes 22 commodities and it is traded as a future on the Chicago Mercentile Exchange.

It weights energy products at about 55 percent, grains and soft commodities around 25 percent, base and precious metals 10 percent and livestock 10 percent and a typical fund portfolio may roughly match the make up of the index. "We are not repositioning our fund for 1997 because it is designed to give long term exposure to commodities," said Barclays Global Investors' John Demain.

"Last financial year to Oct 31, 1996 its value showed a profit of 30.4 percent and year to date is showing 14.30 percent -- and we are certainly anticipating a double digit performance in the next 12 months," he said.
He added that commodities are going to be a strong market sector to the end of the century.

"Equity (funds) tend to concentrate on metals and energy as there are equities there to invest in. There aren't the same number of companies where you can get exposure to agricultural commodities," Demain said.
The "gearing" between moves in the underlying metal prices, especially gold, can signifcantly impact the share price, analysts added.

"A small move (like gold's mini rally at the beginning of November) of about $2-$3, or one percent, tends to see a gearing of about five times because gold mine cash costs average about $270-$280," said mining share analyst Roger Chaplin at stockbrokers T. Hoare and Co.

Nevertheless all mining shares underperformed in 1996 compared with other sectors. "We hope that in 1997 if metal prices improve, they will change that pattern," said Graham Birch at Mercury Asset Management.
"A 25-percent rise in the gold price could lead to a 100 percent rise in the company's profit per ounce. The gearing effect shows up quite clearly in gold," he added.
"But hedging forward prices removes these options. That's why hedging is so damaging for mining shares," Birch added.
Average mining costs for copper miners vary much more, from around 25 cents per lb to 70 cents, Chaplin said.

"But major companies like MIM and RTZ for example have other things (contributing to profit) as well so income is much more spread than for a gold mine which decreases the impact of price moves," he said.
Even so, Ian Henderson of Fleming Natural Resources is preparing to alter the asset allocation in his equity-based fund to reflect an acceleration in demand for industrial commodities.
"We have been quite long in precious metals which might not be such a beneficiary of this scenario," he said.
After very good performances in 1996, energy-related stocks are also likely to be trimmed for next year. "They are likely to match the indices and not do anything much else," he said.
Henderson proposed raising his holdings in base metal and other industrial commodity shares by about 10 percent to 45 percent next year.
Energy will come down to about 30 percent from 40 percent and precious metals to about 30 percent from 35 percent.
